# Rule reference

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen_rules_doc.py from src/txwarden/rules.py. Do not edit. -->

TxWarden ships **55 rules**. Severity is fixed per rule and decides the verdict: **CRITICAL -> BLOCK** (26 rules), **HIGH -> WARN** (21 rules), **MEDIUM and INFO -> ALLOW** (8 rules, reported but never stopping). The verdict is the worst severity among the findings. Tune behaviour through the policy knobs listed under each rule (see [Configuration](../README.md#configuration)) or switch a rule off with `disabled_rules` (except `ENGINE_ERROR` and `SIMULATION_UNAVAILABLE`, which implement fail-closed behaviour and cannot be disabled).

Use `txwarden rules` to list them and `txwarden explain <RULE>` for the text below.

## Target and addresses

### ADDRESS_LOOKALIKE

**Address-poisoning lookalike** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* A counterparty address (spender, operator, recipient or the call target) is not known to the user but shares its first `lookalike_prefix` and last `lookalike_suffix` hex characters with an address that is (trust lists, address book, the sender).

*Why it matters.* Address poisoning sends dust from a vanity address that matches the start and end of an address you use, hoping you copy it from your history. Wallets show only those characters, so the two look identical. Compare the full address. A genuine second address of yours that happens to collide must be added to the address book to stop the finding.

*Policy knobs:* `lookalike_prefix` (default 4), `lookalike_suffix` (default 4), `address_book` (default empty), `trusted_spenders` (default empty), `trusted_recipients` (default empty)

### DENYLISTED_TARGET

**Call to a denylisted contract** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The transaction's `to` address is on the user's denylist.

*Why it matters.* Put known drainers, sanctioned addresses and contracts you were phished by on `denylist`. Do not sign; there is no benign reading of a call to an address you have already marked bad.

*Policy knobs:* `denylist` (default empty)

### CALL_TO_NON_CONTRACT

**Calldata sent to an address with no code** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The transaction carries calldata but `to` has no deployed code (checked with eth_getCode).

*Why it matters.* A call to an address without code always succeeds and does nothing, while any attached ETH is simply transferred. Typical causes: a wrong-network address, a mistyped contract, a contract that was self-destructed. Verify the address on the intended chain.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_call_to_non_contract` (default True)

## ERC-20 approvals

### APPROVAL_TO_DENYLISTED

**Approval to denylisted spender** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* Any approval whose spender is on the denylist.

*Why it matters.* Do not sign. If you already did, revoke the allowance.

*Policy knobs:* `denylist` (default empty)

### UNLIMITED_APPROVAL_UNKNOWN

**Unlimited approval to unknown spender** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* An ERC-20 or Permit2 approval of 2**128 raw units or more (larger than any real token's total supply, so effectively unlimited; covers uint256/uint160/uint128 maxima) to a spender that is not in `trusted_spenders`.

*Why it matters.* This is the primary drainer primitive: once granted, the spender can move the whole balance at any time, including long after you have forgotten the site. Approve an exact amount instead or trust the spender explicitly after verifying it.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### APPROVAL_UNKNOWN_SPENDER

**Bounded approval to unknown spender** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* A finite, non-zero approval to a spender that is not in `trusted_spenders`.

*Why it matters.* A bounded approval limits the loss to the amount, but the spender is still someone you have not vetted. Check the address against the dapp's documentation before signing.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### UNLIMITED_APPROVAL_TRUSTED

**Unlimited approval to trusted spender** - MEDIUM -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* Unlimited approval to an address in `trusted_spenders`.

*Why it matters.* Reported so the explanation can mention it; the verdict stays ALLOW because you trusted the spender. Prefer exact approvals even for trusted spenders; a trusted contract can be upgraded.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### APPROVAL_REVOKED

**Approval set to zero** - INFO -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* An allowance is being set to zero.

*Why it matters.* Revocations are safe and encouraged; reported for completeness.

## NFT operator approvals

### OPERATOR_APPROVAL_DENYLISTED

**setApprovalForAll to denylisted operator** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The operator of a `setApprovalForAll(…, true)` is on the denylist.

*Why it matters.* Do not sign.

*Policy knobs:* `denylist` (default empty)

### OPERATOR_APPROVAL_UNKNOWN

**setApprovalForAll to unknown operator** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* `setApprovalForAll(operator, true)` on an ERC-721/1155 collection where the operator is not in `trusted_operators` or `trusted_spenders`.

*Why it matters.* Grants the operator control of every token in the collection, now and in the future. This is how NFT drainers work, and there is no 'bounded' variant. Only approve marketplaces you chose to use, and revoke afterwards.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_operators` (default empty), `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### OPERATOR_APPROVAL_TRUSTED

**setApprovalForAll to trusted operator** - MEDIUM -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* Collection-wide approval to an operator you trust (marketplace or aggregator).

*Why it matters.* Allowed, but reported: a trusted marketplace can still be compromised or upgraded. Revoke when you stop trading.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_operators` (default empty), `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### OPERATOR_APPROVAL_REVOKED

**Operator approval revoked** - INFO -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* `setApprovalForAll(operator, false)`.

*Why it matters.* Safe; reported for completeness.

## Signature permits

### PERMIT_TO_DENYLISTED

**Permit to denylisted spender** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* A permit whose spender is on the denylist.

*Why it matters.* Do not sign.

*Policy knobs:* `denylist` (default empty)

### PERMIT_UNLIMITED_UNKNOWN

**Unlimited permit to unknown spender** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* An EIP-2612, DAI-style or Permit2 signature granting an unlimited allowance to a spender that is not trusted.

*Why it matters.* Permits are gasless and happen off-chain, so a phishing page can collect one without any on-chain transaction and drain you later. Never sign an unlimited permit for a spender you did not verify.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### PERMIT_FAR_DEADLINE

**Permit or allowance valid for a very long time** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* A permit's deadline, or a Permit2 allowance's expiration, is more than `permit_deadline_warn_s` after the block time (default 30 days) or effectively never expires.

*Why it matters.* Long-lived signatures get harvested and replayed later, often after the site that asked for them is compromised. Ask for a short deadline.

*Policy knobs:* `permit_deadline_warn_s` (default 2592000)

### PERMIT_UNKNOWN_SPENDER

**Bounded permit to unknown spender** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* A finite permit to a spender that is not trusted.

*Why it matters.* The loss is bounded by the amount, but a signature cannot be revoked by an on-chain transaction until it has been used or expired (except by bumping the nonce).

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### PERMIT_UNLIMITED_TRUSTED

**Unlimited permit to trusted spender** - MEDIUM -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* An unlimited permit to a trusted spender.

*Why it matters.* Allowed, but reported; prefer exact amounts.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

## Transfers and recipients

### TRANSFER_TO_DENYLISTED

**Transfer to denylisted address** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* Funds are sent to an address on the denylist.

*Why it matters.* Do not sign.

*Policy knobs:* `denylist` (default empty)

### NEAR_FULL_BALANCE_TO_NEW_ADDRESS

**Near-full balance to unrecognised address** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* At least `drain_fraction` (default 90%) of the sender's balance of the token goes to an address that is not in `trusted_recipients` or the address book.

*Why it matters.* Emptying a wallet into an address you have never used is what a drain looks like. If it is a deliberate migration, add the destination to `trusted_recipients` first.

*Policy knobs:* `drain_fraction` (default 0.9), `trusted_recipients` (default empty)

### SWAP_RECIPIENT_MISMATCH

**Swap or router output sent to a third party** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The recipient of a swap (`to`), of a Universal Router SWEEP/TRANSFER/PAY_PORTION/UNWRAP/WRAP, of added or removed V2 liquidity, or of an NFPM `collect` is not the sender, the router itself, a trusted recipient or a labelled address.

*Why it matters.* A drainer can ask you to swap your own tokens and route the proceeds to the attacker, which looks like an ordinary swap in most wallet UIs. Swap UIs that route a fee portion to their own address also trip this; add that address to `trusted_recipients`.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_swap_recipient_mismatch` (default True), `trusted_recipients` (default empty), `address_book` (default empty)

### TRANSFER_TO_BURN_ADDRESS

**Transfer to the zero or dead address** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The recipient is 0x000…000 or 0x000…dEaD.

*Why it matters.* Funds sent there are unrecoverable. Intentional burns are rare; confirm the intent.

### TRANSFER_TO_FRESH_ADDRESS

**Transfer to a never-used address** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The recipient has no code, nonce 0 and zero ETH balance.

*Why it matters.* Fresh addresses are typical of poisoning and typo'd destinations; legitimate new wallets are usually funded first. Send a small test amount, or add the address to `trusted_recipients`.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_fresh_recipients` (default True), `trusted_recipients` (default empty)

### TRANSFER_TO_TOKEN_CONTRACT

**Tokens sent to the token's own contract** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The recipient of a token transfer is the token contract itself.

*Why it matters.* Almost no token can return tokens sent to its own address; the funds are lost. Usually a copy-paste of the wrong field in a wallet UI.

### TRANSFER_TO_UNKNOWN_CONTRACT

**Token transfer to unknown contract** - MEDIUM -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* Tokens (not ETH) are sent to a contract that is not in the address book.

*Why it matters.* Tokens sent directly to a contract are often unrecoverable. Reported, not blocked, because deposits into vaults and bridges do this legitimately.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_contract_recipients` (default True)

## Swaps (price impact, slippage, MEV)

### LIQUIDITY_EXHAUSTED

**Pool cannot fill the trade** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The Uniswap V3 pool runs out of in-range liquidity before the input is consumed (fill fraction below `min_fill_fraction`).

*Why it matters.* The swap would revert or be partially filled. Reduce the size or route differently.

*Policy knobs:* `min_fill_fraction` (default 0.999)

### PRICE_IMPACT_EXTREME

**Extreme price impact** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* Execution price is at least `impact_block_bps` (default 20%) worse than the pool's spot price.

*Why it matters.* The trade is moving the pool so much that most of the value is lost to the curve. Split it, use a deeper pool, or use a limit order.

*Policy knobs:* `impact_block_bps` (default 2000)

### SANDWICH_EXPOSURE_SEVERE

**Severe sandwich exposure** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* A searcher can extract at least `sandwich_block_bps` (default 1%) of the input by front- and back-running within the slippage floor, computed by optimising the front-run size on the pool curve (V2, multi-hop V2 and V3 with ticks).

*Why it matters.* This is an estimate for a single-pool sandwich before gas and competition; real extraction can be lower (gas, competition) or higher (multi-block strategies). Tighten the floor or use a protected RPC.

*Policy knobs:* `sandwich_block_bps` (default 100)

### SLIPPAGE_TOLERANCE_EXTREME

**Extreme slippage tolerance** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* `min_out` is at least `slippage_block` (default 5%) below the simulated output.

*Why it matters.* Anything between the simulated output and your floor can be taken by a searcher sandwiching the trade. Tighten the tolerance.

*Policy knobs:* `slippage_block` (default 0.05)

### PRICE_IMPACT_HIGH

**High price impact** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* Price impact is at least `impact_warn_bps` (default 5%).

*Why it matters.* A large share of the trade is paid to the curve rather than a fair price.

*Policy knobs:* `impact_warn_bps` (default 500)

### SANDWICH_EXPOSURE

**Sandwich exposure** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The extractable amount is at least `sandwich_warn_bps` (default 0.3%).

*Why it matters.* See SANDWICH_EXPOSURE_SEVERE.

*Policy knobs:* `sandwich_warn_bps` (default 30)

### SLIPPAGE_TOLERANCE_LOOSE

**Loose slippage tolerance** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* `min_out` is at least `slippage_warn` (default 0.75%) below the simulated output.

*Why it matters.* A looser floor leaves room for MEV extraction; tighten it or use a private mempool.

*Policy knobs:* `slippage_warn` (default 0.0075)

## Simulation health

### CHAIN_ID_MISMATCH

**Chain id mismatch** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The transaction's chain id differs from `expected_chain_id` in the policy or, when that is unset, from the chain the simulator is connected to.

*Why it matters.* A signature produced for one chain can be replayed or mis-sent on another, and a simulation on the wrong chain says nothing about what will happen. Reconnect the simulator to the right network or fix the transaction's chain id.

*Policy knobs:* `expected_chain_id` (default None)

### ENGINE_ERROR

**A rule check crashed** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* An internal check raised an exception while evaluating this transaction.

*Why it matters.* Fail closed: an engine fault must never turn into ALLOW. Please report it with the transaction and simulation JSON.

### GAS_EXTREME

**Extreme gas usage** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* Estimated gas exceeds `gas_block_absolute` (default 10,000,000).

*Why it matters.* Looping drainers and griefing contracts burn gas to extract value from the signer. Legitimate wallet interactions almost never approach this.

*Policy knobs:* `gas_block_absolute` (default 10000000)

### SIMULATION_UNAVAILABLE

**Simulation could not be performed** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The simulator reported an infrastructure error (RPC unreachable, timeout, HTTP error, malformed response, pruned state).

*Why it matters.* TxWarden fails closed: with no analysis there is nothing to base ALLOW on. Fix connectivity (see the troubleshooting guide), then re-run.

### ANALYSIS_INCOMPLETE

**Swap or liquidity analysis could not run** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The call is a swap or liquidity removal but the pool state needed to evaluate price impact, sandwich exposure or the removed share was not available (no RPC configured, pool not found, or an unsupported route such as a multi-hop V3 path).

*Why it matters.* The rules that would have checked this trade could not run, so the result is WARN rather than ALLOW. Configure an RPC, or disable the rule if you accept static-only review.

### ETH_REJECTED_BY_CONTRACT

**Contract rejects plain ETH** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The call reverts, ETH is attached, and the target also reverts on a plain value transfer.

*Why it matters.* The contract has no payable receive/fallback, so the attached ETH cannot be accepted. Send the ETH through a function that accepts it, or to a different address.

### GAS_ABNORMAL

**Abnormal gas usage** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* Estimated gas exceeds `gas_abnormal_multiple` (default 5x) times the typical cost of this kind of call (table in `risk.TYPICAL_GAS`, 250k for unrecognised calls).

*Why it matters.* A simple approval that costs 900k gas is doing something else. Investigate with a trace.

*Policy knobs:* `gas_abnormal_multiple` (default 5)

### REVERT

**Transaction reverts in simulation** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The simulated call reverted (the revert reason is included when the node returns one).

*Why it matters.* Signing a transaction that reverts wastes gas and may indicate the wrong network, stale parameters or a trap. Read the reason; do not sign until it simulates successfully.

### CHECKS_SKIPPED

**Some optional checks did not run** - INFO -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* The simulator reported checks it could not perform (account probes, honeypot probe, call trace, or all chain-state checks in static mode).

*Why it matters.* Transparency only: the verdict is computed from what was available. Use a node that supports `debug_traceCall` and `eth_simulateV1` for full coverage.

## Call tree

### DELEGATECALL_TO_UNKNOWN

**Nested delegatecall to unknown code** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* A contract below the top level delegatecalls into code that is not in the address book, `trusted_implementations` or `trusted_spenders`.

*Why it matters.* Delegatecall runs foreign code against the caller's storage and balances. A drainer wrapped in a proxy uses it to hide the sweep logic. Add known libraries to `trusted_implementations`.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_unknown_delegatecall` (default True), `trusted_implementations` (default empty), `address_book` (default empty)

### DENYLISTED_IN_TRACE

**Denylisted address touched in call tree** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* A frame below the top level calls a denylisted address.

*Why it matters.* Do not sign; the transaction interacts with a known-bad address indirectly.

*Policy knobs:* `denylist` (default empty)

### SELFDESTRUCT_IN_TRACE

**SELFDESTRUCT in call tree** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The call tree contains a SELFDESTRUCT frame.

*Why it matters.* Self-destructing contracts are used to hide code and sweep balances. Legitimate flows that touch user funds rarely need it.

### CONTRACT_CREATION_IN_TRACE

**Contract created during the call** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* CREATE or CREATE2 inside a transaction.

*Why it matters.* Fresh contracts can't be vetted by address. Expected for factories and account abstraction; unexpected for an approval or swap.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_contract_creation` (default True)

### UNTRUSTED_PULL_IN_TRACE

**Untrusted contract moves your tokens to a third party** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* A transfer out of the sender's account (``transferFrom``, a Permit2 pull) is initiated by a contract that is not trusted or labelled, and its recipient is neither the sender, that contract, nor a known address. Found both in the decoded call and in the call tree (``debug_traceCall``), where opaque contracts hide it.

*Why it matters.* This is how an 'airdrop claim' or 'verify wallet' contract empties an account using an allowance granted earlier. Unlabelled aggregators and vaults trip it too; add them to `trusted_spenders` once vetted.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty), `trusted_recipients` (default empty), `address_book` (default empty)

### PROXY_DELEGATECALL_UNKNOWN_IMPL

**Proxy delegates to unlabelled implementation** - MEDIUM -> ALLOW

*When it fires.* The target itself delegatecalls to an implementation that is not labelled.

*Why it matters.* Normal for upgradeable proxies; reported so the implementation can be reviewed.

*Policy knobs:* `flag_unknown_delegatecall` (default True)

## Honeypot probe

### HONEYPOT_SELL_REVERTS

**Token can be bought but not sold** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The buy-then-sell probe succeeds on the buy and reverts on the sell, including the fee-on-transfer sell variant.

*Why it matters.* Classic honeypot: the token lets you in and not out. Run on a node with `eth_simulateV1`; with only router quotes the probe cannot see transfer-restriction logic.

### ROUND_TRIP_LOSS_SEVERE

**Severe round-trip loss** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* Buying then immediately selling loses at least `honeypot_loss_block` (default 25%) of the input.

*Why it matters.* A transfer tax or rigged pool takes the difference. Ordinary round trips lose about twice the pool fee plus impact.

*Policy knobs:* `honeypot_loss_block` (default 0.25)

### ROUND_TRIP_LOSS

**Round-trip loss (fee on transfer)** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The round trip loses at least `honeypot_loss_warn` (default 5%), more than fees and impact explain.

*Why it matters.* Likely a fee-on-transfer token; the effective price is worse than quoted.

*Policy knobs:* `honeypot_loss_warn` (default 0.05)

## Liquidity removal

### LP_REMOVAL_MAJORITY

**Removes the majority of a pool's liquidity** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The call withdraws at least `lp_removal_block_fraction` (default 50%) of the pool.

*Why it matters.* Rug pulls look like this. So does closing your own single-LP pool; if that is the case, disable the rule for this transaction.

*Policy knobs:* `lp_removal_block_fraction` (default 0.5)

### LP_REMOVAL_LARGE

**Removes a large share of a pool's liquidity** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* The call withdraws at least `lp_removal_warn_fraction` (default 20%) of the pool.

*Why it matters.* Large removals precede or accompany rugs; check who holds the position.

*Policy knobs:* `lp_removal_warn_fraction` (default 0.2)

## Cross-transaction (bundle) rules

### BUNDLE_ADD_THEN_REMOVE_LIQUIDITY

**Add then remove liquidity in one bundle** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* Liquidity is added to and removed from the same pool within the bundle.

*Why it matters.* Launch-and-rug choreography; also a pointless way to burn gas for a normal user.

### BUNDLE_APPROVE_THEN_PULL

**Approval then pull by the same unknown spender** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* One transaction in the bundle approves (or permits) an unknown spender and a later one calls that spender, has it as the transferFrom operator, or has it in the call tree.

*Why it matters.* Drainer flows split the approval from the pull so each step looks harmless in isolation. Review the bundle as a whole; do not sign.

*Policy knobs:* `trusted_spenders` (default empty)

### BUNDLE_MIXED_CHAIN_IDS

**Bundle mixes chain ids** - CRITICAL -> BLOCK

*When it fires.* The transactions in the bundle target different chain ids.

*Why it matters.* A bundle is one decision; mixed chains usually mean a mis-assembled or malicious request.

### BUNDLE_CUMULATIVE_DRAIN

**Bundle drains the balance cumulatively** - HIGH -> WARN

*When it fires.* Individual transfers stay under `drain_fraction` but together they exceed it for a token.

*Why it matters.* Splitting a drain into several smaller transfers evades the per-transaction check.

*Policy knobs:* `drain_fraction` (default 0.9)
